objectives: Reach a negotiated settlement with the UK that avoids UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU exports.
Prevent the UK from joining a coordinated retaliation/dispute with Japan and Korea over the FTA-disapplication provision.
Preserve the core architecture of the EU measure (bound rate of 50%, TRQ mechanism, rationale of responding to non-market-economy overcapacity) so it is not seen to unravel under pressure.
Avoid setting a precedent in the UK settlement that Turkey, Korea, Japan or India could then demand be matched, given their larger volumes.
Secure something the Commission can present to the Council and member states as a genuine, WTO-consistent negotiation in good faith, allowing the June timetable to hold.
Protect the ongoing Geneva working relationship with the UK delegation across other goods files.
If possible, extract reciprocal value from the UK's own steel safeguard and Article XXVIII process (e.g. EU exporter quota treatment) as part of an overall package, not just one-way compensation.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement (or a de facto understanding even short of full capital sign-off) in which the UK accepts a defined, secure share of the TRQ or equivalent compensation, does not withdraw concessions, and does not join a Japan/Korea coalition against the FTA-disapplication clause — while the EU's underlying measure and June timetable remain intact and other claimants are not handed a stronger precedent than intended. Failure is a breakdown that leads to UK retaliation, UK alignment with Japan/Korea against the EU on FTA treatment, a Council fight over an unfinished Geneva process, or a settlement so generous it invites Turkey/Korea/Japan/India to demand equivalent treatment and destabilises the whole package.
declaration.approach: Treat this as a genuine negotiation, not a formality, since Brussels needs a credible account of good-faith engagement and I need to manage a long relationship with my UK counterpart. Start by probing what the UK actually values most — secure volume, a country-specific share, protection from the FTA-disapplication clause given the TCA relationship, or a review/duration clause — rather than assuming price is the only lever. Use the UK's parallel safeguard and Article XXVIII process as a natural venue for reciprocal trade-offs (EU exporter treatment under the UK measure) so compensation isn't purely one-directional. Be careful not to move on the headline TRQ volume or bound rate quickly, since those are the parts most likely to be watched by other claimants; look instead for solutions in allocation method, country share carve-outs, FTA/TCA treatment, and review clauses, which are more containable and harder for Turkey/Korea/Japan to piggyback on. Keep Brussels informed each round with a clear recommendation, flagging the coalition risk explicitly so capital understands the strategic value of an early, contained settlement versus a cheaper but more exposed one reached late or not at all. Avoid language at the table that could be read as EU concessions to non-market-economy pressure being negotiable — keep that rationale firm even while flexing implementation details.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A secure, predictable share of the TRQ (likely country-specific rather than global first-come-first-served given UK's concentrated production and fear of being crowded out by Turkey/Korea), exemption or softening of the FTA-disapplication clause given the TCA relationship, protection or leverage for UK producers who are politically sensitive due to concentrated local employment, and reciprocal treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard measure. They will also want a credible claim to have secured compensation without appearing to have let the EU set a precedent that weakens their own upcoming measure.

Conclusion by June with the measure's core structure intact, a negotiation that can be presented as good-faith Article XXVIII compliance, protection of steel-producing member states' interests, but also awareness from steel-consuming member states that excessive tariffs raise input costs. They will not want a settlement that becomes the template for Turkey/Korea (larger volumes) or that appears to reward NME-adjacent free-riding via UK re-export risk.

Larger absolute volumes protected, likely pursuing their own country-specific shares; they are watching the UK settlement as a possible benchmark and may support UK positioning that increases overall TRQ volume or shifts allocation toward country shares, which would help them too.

Protection of its narrower but valuable trade, and appears to be probing a coalition with Korea to pressure the UK into joint FTA retaliation against the EU's FTA-disapplication clause — a strategic risk I need to defuse by making the UK's own bilateral outcome satisfactory enough that joining such a coalition looks unnecessary or risky to the UK's own separate interests (e.g. its TCA relationship with the EU).

A substantial interest consultation only; likely seeking assurance of continued market access and possibly a modest carve-out, lower stakes for this specific negotiation but relevant to the precedent-setting concern.

objectives: Secure a settlement with the UK that allows Council to vote on the modification in June, avoiding a no-deal outcome that delays implementation past the deadline.

Preserve a workable, enforceable import regime: a meaningful bound rate increase and a TRQ that materially reduces current tariff-free tonnage entering the EU market, particularly from non-market-economy sources.
Avoid establishing a country-specific UK carve-out or quota share so generous that it undermines the global TRQ's integrity or invites similar demands from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.
Retain flexibility on the FTA-disapplication clause as a bargaining chip rather than a fixed red line — trade it for UK concessions on quota administration, duration, or review clauses.
Manage the linkage with the UK's own steel safeguard: seek reasonable treatment for EU exporters under UK country allocations as part of the compensation package, reducing net cost to EU industry.
Keep member states (steel producers vs. downstream consumers) and the Trade Policy Committee onside so Council approval is not put at risk by the terms agreed.
Minimise the risk of additional retaliation or destabilisation given the parallel US tariff threat — do not let this negotiation become a second front.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a concluded agreement by the round deadline that includes a bound rate materially above zero, a TRQ that constrains UK tariff-free volume well below the historical 2.4mt baseline (or an equivalent value-based compensation), no unconstrained UK-specific quota that becomes a precedent, and some reciprocal accommodation on the UK's own safeguard for EU exporters. Failure: no deal (measure proceeds as notified, UK retaliates, Council vote proceeds but EU faces WTO friction and a damaged relationship with a major partner), or a deal so generous to the UK that it fails to deliver a real import reduction and draws Council/member-state objections, or a deal that provokes Turkey/Korea/India/Japan to escalate their own claims by citing UK treatment as a benchmark.
declaration.approach: Open firm on the core architecture (50% out-of-quota rate, global TRQ, FCFS) to anchor expectations, since this is what I have a mandate to defend. Use the FTA-disapplication clause and quota volume/allocation method as the primary negotiating currency — these are areas I can move without conceding the core regime. Signal early that a UK-specific carve-out is politically costly for me domestically (steel-producing member states will object) unless it's modest and matched by UK reciprocity on their own safeguard treatment of EU exporters. Push for a review clause rather than a large volume concession, since it preserves my ability to tighten the regime later without a permanent large TRQ. Use the credible threat of the June deadline and the UK's asymmetric exposure to extract movement, but avoid overplaying this since a collapsed negotiation creates real reputational and retaliation risk for the EU too (US pressure already live). Sequence concessions: hold the headline rate and volume until late rounds, trade administrative and product-line details early to build momentum toward a deal.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A UK-specific quota share (not pure global FCFS) sized close to their historical 2.4mt trade, a lower or phased-in out-of-quota rate, carve-outs for their concentrated product lines (e.g., specific plate/coil grades), preservation of FTA-equivalent treatment given the TCA relationship, and reciprocal favourable treatment for UK exporters under any residual access — plus something to show their steel-producing constituencies to justify not retaliating.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (e.g., France, Germany, Italy, Spain)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff protection, minimal TRQ volume, no generous UK carve-out, strong anti-circumvention text, and disapplication of FTA benefits to non-EEA partners including the UK.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Sufficient tariff-free volume and administrative simplicity (licensing vs FCFS congestion) to avoid input cost spikes; may push back against too restrictive a regime.

Comparable or better treatment than the UK secures; will use any generous UK settlement as a benchmark to demand similar country shares or compensation, so I need to avoid setting an expensive precedent.
Not a direct party, but threatening retaliation over the EU's broader steel Article XXVIII actions — increases my incentive to conclude quickly and avoid multiplying fronts of trade conflict.
A concluded, defensible deal by June that can be presented as protecting EU industry while maintaining the EU's reputation as a rules-based, negotiation-willing WTO member.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) that reflects historical UK export volumes (~2.4mt), protecting against being crowded out by Turkey/Korea who ship larger volumes
Preserve or restore TCA-consistent treatment for UK steel, resisting or narrowing the disapplication of FTA tariff reductions as applied to the UK specifically
Push out-of-quota rate and quota volume to a landing zone that keeps UK exporters commercially viable, not just nominally 'zero duty in-quota'
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so this isn't a permanent settlement locked in at a bad baseline
Explore compensation on other EU schedule lines as an alternative/supplement if quota volume/share can't move far enough
Avoid a no-deal outcome that triggers UK retaliation, given UK also needs EU cooperation on UK's own steel safeguard and Article XXVIII process (EU exporters hold quota there)
Keep Japan/Korea sympathetic but avoid being drawn into a joint FTA retaliation dispute that would blow up the UK-EU relationship and timeline before UK has secured its own bilateral terms
Protect the working relationship with EU Geneva counterpart across the broader goods file, since this negotiation is not the only file we work together on
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement with a UK-specific TRQ share materially above pro-rata FCFS exposure, meaningful preservation of TCA preference (or equivalent compensation), an out-of-quota rate and volume that keeps UK exporters trading at real commercial volumes, and a review clause within a few years - concluded without triggering retaliation cycles. Partial success: no deal in Geneva but UK preserves optionality to retaliate proportionately and uses the six-month window to extract better terms via UK's own steel measure/TCA leverage. Failure: settling for terms barely better than the EU's opening offer, losing TCA preference outright with no compensation, or a collapse into an uncoordinated multi-front trade dispute (with Japan/Korea) that damages the broader Geneva relationship and UK leverage on its own safeguard process.
declaration.approach: Start firm but constructive: table the actual trade and employment stakes clearly, anchor on a country-specific allocation methodology (historical trade share) rather than global FCFS, and use the TCA relationship as leverage - noting the EU's proposal to disapply FTA treatment cuts against the spirit of a negotiated bilateral relationship and invites UK reciprocal action on our own steel safeguard where EU holds allocations. Avoid making our red lines explicit early; probe the EU's actual flexibility on volume, allocation, and review clause before revealing our own landing zone. Use the multi-round structure to test movement round by round rather than front-loading demands. Keep formal engagement with Japan/Korea correct and useful for information purposes but decline to commit to joint retaliation, since our best leverage is the credible, calibrated threat of independent UK action tied to our own TRQ/safeguard process, not a multilateral pile-on that removes flexibility and slows things down. Report faithfully to London each round, flagging where EU movement is real versus cosmetic, and let capital set the actual settlement bar since I have not been given a fixed figure.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclude by June to meet the Council timeline, ideally with minimal change to the notified measure; wants to protect EU steel producers from Chinese/non-market-economy overcapacity while managing internal member-state divisions between producers and consumers; will resist opening country-specific shares too generously for fear of setting precedent for Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims; may have some flexibility on review clause and product carve-outs as cheaper concessions than volume/share changes.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Protect UK steel jobs and production sites concentrated in specific constituencies; wants meaningful compensation or a workable TRQ share; will be cautious about triggering a trade war with the EU given wider TCA relationship; may want to use UK's own steel safeguard as a bargaining chip; ultimately needs a deal that is politically defensible domestically.

Want the UK to join a joint FTA retaliation/dispute to pressure the EU on the FTA-disapplication clause, since they have their own principal supplying interests and FTA-adjacent exposure; want to maximise collective leverage against the EU's steel regime; will keep pushing UK to commit rather than negotiate quietly bilaterally.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (as principal supplying interests in the EU process)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger volume shippers than the UK, likely pushing for the largest possible country-specific shares or, failing that, a global FCFS system that favours their scale advantage over the UK's narrower product range.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Want to limit the out-of-quota rate and keep supply flowing (including from the UK) to avoid input cost inflation for their manufacturers, creating potential internal EU allies for a softer landing zone.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-producing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Want the tightest possible measure - low quota, high out-of-quota tariff, no generous UK-specific carve-outs - to protect domestic production from all import sources including the UK.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK quota share within the EU TRQ (not pure global first-come-first-served), sized against the UK's historical 2.4Mt trade to preserve the bulk of tariff-free access
Preserve UK access on the product lines most critical to the plants at risk of closure (avoid carve-outs that disadvantage narrow UK product mix)
Prevent the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for the UK specifically — resist being treated worse than other FTA partners given the TCA relationship
Obtain a manageable out-of-quota rate or phased approach rather than a cliff-edge 50%
Secure a review clause and reasonable duration so the regime isn't a permanent settlement of UK access on unfavourable terms
Preserve flexibility to use UK safeguard country-specific quota concessions to EU as a bargaining chip, not a giveaway
Avoid a breakdown that forces reliance solely on retaliation/withdrawal, which is slow (6-month delay) and doesn't help plants facing imminent closure
Keep option of subsidisation in reserve — do not signal to EU that UK has a safety net that reduces urgency
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a UK-specific quota share meaningfully above what pure global FCFS would likely deliver to the UK (protecting most of the £3bn/2.4Mt trade), continued TCA tariff preference maintained, a review clause and workable out-of-quota rate, achieved via reciprocal but limited concessions on the UK's own safeguard quota for EU exporters. Failure: EU proceeds with global FCFS TRQ and FTA disapplication as originally notified, UK share of the 400kt quota is eroded by faster-moving competitors (Turkey/Korea), no review clause, and UK is left only with slow, generally damaging retaliatory withdrawal as recourse while plants close in the interim.
declaration.approach: Move early to reframe the negotiation from 'accept EU's opening offer' to 'design the allocation method,' since country-specific allocation is where UK's principal-supplying-interest status has the most leverage — the UK cannot easily change the 400kt volume or the 50% out-of-quota rate alone, but can make a strong legal and factual case for country shares given large, stable historical volumes. Use the parallel UK safeguard process as a genuine trading chip: offer improved country-specific allocations for EU exporters in the UK's own measure in exchange for a defined UK-specific share and preservation of TCA treatment. Avoid revealing the subsidisation fallback to keep pressure on EU to make real concessions. Escalate concessions gradually across rounds, holding back most valuable offers (safeguard quota improvements) until later rounds to test EU flexibility first on cost-free asks (review clause, product line definitions, transitional phase-in).

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A workable, WTO-defensible TRQ that protects EU producers from non-market-economy overcapacity, minimal compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule, and a settlement that can clear Council approval quickly given the June deadline — likely resistant to generous country-specific carve-outs for UK given similar pressure from Turkey/Korea claims, but may value swift closure over holding out for the maximalist global FCFS position given the June deadline and multiple parallel claims to manage.

Maximise UK-specific protected access, protect the specific plants at risk, avoid setting a precedent that undermines the UK's own safeguard measure, and reach a deal that can be sold to ministers as protecting steel jobs without appearing to have capitulated to EU demands on FTA treatment.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (not at this table but relevant)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Larger country-specific shares than the UK given greater volumes; their parallel claims may harden the EU's reluctance to grant the UK a generous share, since any UK-specific allocation could be a template Turkey/Korea will demand be matched or bettered.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council mandate)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A strict, protective TRQ regime, low volumes, high out-of-quota rate, minimal exceptions — pushing the Commission toward the harder end of its mandate.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Sufficient quota volume and reasonable out-of-quota rates to avoid input cost spikes, potentially a moderating influence on the Commission's mandate that the UK could indirectly benefit from.
Maximum protected tariff-free access to the EU market, ideally a fixed UK-specific quota at or near historical volumes, to make continued investment viable.
Continued access to EU steel inputs under the UK's own safeguard measure without new restrictions, which constrains how much DBT can concede in the reciprocal offer to the EU.

public_message: The EU confirms it is opening this Article XXVIII negotiation with the UK as a principal supplying interest. Our formal notification stands as tabled: a bound rate of 50% ad valorem with a global TRQ of 400,000 tonnes administered first-come first-served, and disapplication of FTA tariff preferences for non-EEA partners including the UK. That said, we recognise the UK's exposure is concentrated and different in character from Turkey's or Korea's, and we are willing to discuss a country-specific tranche within the pool, the administration method, and a review clause as part of a compensation package. We are also willing to discuss the interaction of the FTA-disapplication provision with the TCA specifically, separate from how it applies to other partners. We'd like to hear the UK's read on scale and structure before we move further.

other_terms: FTA disapplication as notified applies to all non-EEA FTA partners including the UK
Willing to discuss a UK-specific tranche in a later round
Willing to discuss TCA-specific treatment of the FTA disapplication clause
No product-line carve-outs proposed at this stage

expectations.why: We need to see how far apart we are on volume and structure before Brussels will consider moving off the notified terms, and we want an early signal on whether the TCA carve-out can keep the UK from aligning with Japan/Korea

private_rationale: Opening at the notified position preserves EU leverage and does not concede structure before hearing the UK's ask. Flagging willingness to discuss a country-specific tranche and the TCA point signals good faith without committing numbers, which should help keep the UK engaged bilaterally rather than drifting toward a joint Japan/Korea FTA retaliation strategy. Holding the out-of-quota rate and pool size firm in round 1 preserves room to make real concessions later and protects the Council timeline by not pre-negotiating against ourselves.

public_message: We welcome the EU's recognition that the UK's position is distinct from Turkey's and Korea's, and its openness to a country-specific tranche, administration method and review clause. But let's be clear on scale: UK exports to the EU have averaged 2.4 million tonnes annually, and the EU is the destination for the large majority of UK production not consumed domestically. A 400,000 tonne global pool, first-come first-served, represents a reduction of well over 80% in the UK's tariff-free access at a stroke — that is not a modification of a concession, it is the effective closure of the UK's principal export market, and it goes well beyond what 'substantially equivalent compensation' can credibly offset after the fact. Our opening position is that any settlement must be measured against that baseline. We would want to see: a total pool sized to reflect genuine EU import need without collapsing UK access, a UK-specific tranche reflecting our historical trade share, licensed rather than first-come-first-served administration so the tranche is actually deliverable to UK exporters rather than front-run by others, an out-of-quota rate materially below 50%, and a review clause on a short cycle given the EU's own domestic legislation is still unsettled. On FTA disapplication: we do not accept that TCA preferences should be disapplied at all — the TCA is a bilateral agreement with its own governance, and folding it into a multilateral overcapacity measure aimed at non-market-economy exporters is not proportionate. We're ready to discuss product-line specifics and circumvention provisions once we have a sense of where the EU can move on volume and rate. We'd also flag, for completeness, that the UK is running its own Article XXVIII process and safeguard review in parallel, and how EU exporters are treated there is naturally linked to how this one lands.

report: Round 1 opening exchange completed. We tabled the notified position (50% bound rate, 400kt global TRQ, FCFS, FTA disapplication for non-EEA partners) but signalled openness to a UK-specific tranche, administration method, review clause, and a distinct look at TCA interaction. UK did not reject the frame outright but set a strong anchor: they characterise 400kt global/FCFS as an ~80%+ cut to their effective access and say this exceeds what compensation can offset. Their opening asks: (1) larger total pool reflecting 'genuine EU import need'; (2) a UK-specific tranche reflecting historical trade share (they will anchor this near their 2.4mt three-year average, though that figure covers all UK-EU steel trade, not just the 41 lines — needs verification); (3) licensed rather than FCFS administration for deliverability; (4) an out-of-quota rate 'materially below' 50%; (5) a short-cycle review clause, citing our own unsettled domestic legislation as justification; (6) full rejection of TCA disapplication — they argue the TCA has its own governance and shouldn't be folded into a multilateral overcapacity measure. They also explicitly linked this to their own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard process affecting EU exporters (3.6mt, 64% of UK imports), signalling that how we land here will affect our treatment there. No hostility, position is exploratory but firm. They did not engage yet on circumvention/product-line detail, holding that back until we move on volume and rate.

recommendation.reasoning: This is only round 1; the UK's opening ask is a maximalist anchor and we should not move toward numbers yet without testing their flexibility further. However, I want capital's authorisation to explore a package broadly in this range for round 2: a materially expanded total pool (not the full 2.4mt UK ask, which conflates all UK-EU steel trade with the 41 affected lines) with a defined UK-specific tranche, administered partly by licence for the country tranche while keeping global FCFS for the residual pool. I recommend holding the out-of-quota rate at 50% for now — conceding on both volume and rate simultaneously in round 1 gives away too much leverage — but flagging a phased reduction as a possible late-stage concession. A review clause at 2-3 years is low-cost for us given our own legislation is unsettled anyway, and costs us little to offer early as a confidence-building move. On TCA: I recommend capital consider decoupling TCA treatment from the broader FTA-disapplication provision entirely, since this is the cheapest concession available to us and directly reduces the risk of a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA retaliation front, which is a bigger strategic risk to us than the tonnage involved.

The real strategic prize for us is preventing a UK-Japan-Korea joint action on FTA disapplication — that is a bigger long-term threat to our multilateral standing and to the broader Goods relationship than a marginal increase in UK's steel tranche. I want to signal enough movement to keep the UK talking bilaterally and away from that coalition, while not over-committing on volume/rate in round 1. I will hold firm on 50% and 400kt as the notified baseline at the table in round 2 opening unless capital gives me room, but I will float the TCA decoupling early since it's cheap and strategically valuable. I am wary of the UK's linkage to their own safeguard/Article XXVIII against EU exporters — that's leverage they will use, and we should treat generous treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure as part of the same package, not a separate track.

instruction: Good round. Move to test the UK's real floor without giving away the store. In Round 2: signal willingness to enlarge the total pool from 400kt toward a range up to roughly 650-750kt (still well short of their 2.4mt bilateral figure, which we should keep noting conflates all UK steel exports, not just the 41 lines at issue). Within that, offer a defined UK-specific country tranche in the 200-250kt range, administered by licence rather than FCFS, with the residual pool remaining global FCFS. Do not name a single final figure yet — present it as a range contingent on their movement on rate and duration. Hold the out-of-quota rate at 50% for now, but you may signal that a phased reduction is discussable if tied to a review clause outcome — do not quantify a lower rate yet. Offer a review clause at 2-3 years as a low-cost concession to build confidence. On the TCA: you are authorised to decouple TCA treatment from the general FTA-disapplication clause — propose that UK-origin steel retain a preferential mechanism inside the UK country tranche (not blanket TCA preservation, but a negotiated carve-out tied to the tranche and to enforcement/anti-circumvention provisions), explicitly to remove this as a shared grievance with Japan/Korea. Make clear none of this is final — it is contingent on the UK engaging seriously on volume, rate and their own parallel measure's treatment of EU exporters. Do not let them read the pool/tranche range as our final offer; frame it as a basis for their counter.

authority.notes: Figures above are a negotiating range for Round 2, not a settlement position — do not present as final. UK tranche to be licensed; residual global pool remains FCFS. Out-of-quota rate held at 50% but you may flag conditional phased reduction tied to review clause outcome, without quantifying yet. TCA: authorised to decouple from blanket FTA-disapplication clause and offer a carved-out preferential mechanism specific to the UK tranche, conditional on robust anti-circumvention text and linkage to how the UK's own parallel measure treats EU exporters. Do not concede on rate and volume simultaneously without capital sign-off. Maintain that UK's 2.4mt figure is not the correct baseline (covers all UK-EU steel trade, not just the 41 lines) — press them for a line-specific figure before moving further.

No numbers were exchanged by either side yet. EU wants our read on scale/structure before moving further — they are fishing for where we'd actually settle.

instruction: Good positioning in Round 1 — hold that line. For Round 2, move from pure principle to a concrete counter-proposal so we control the anchor before the EU does. Table this structure: total global TRQ pool of 2.0 million tonnes (framed as reflecting genuine EU import need, since 400k is a fraction of even non-UK, non-NME-adjacent trade), with a UK-specific country tranche of 1.5 million tonnes carved out within it, licensed administration for the UK tranche (not FCFS), an out-of-quota rate of 15% (opening ask — you can signal flexibility down to around 25% if volume holds), and a review clause at no more than every two years given the EU's own domestic legislation is unsettled. On TCA disapplication: this is a red line, not a trading chip — do not concede it even notionally in exchange for tonnage or rate. Make clear the UK will not accept any construction that treats a bilateral FTA governed by its own dispute mechanism as fair game inside a multilateral overcapacity measure; if the EU wants to preserve the general non-EEA FTA disapplication as leverage over other partners, that is their business, but TCA carve-out is a precondition for any deal with us, not part of the package. You can note, without committing numbers, that improved treatment for EU exporters under our own parallel steel safeguard is available as a concession, but only against real EU movement on tranche size, administration and rate — do not let them get that for free, and do not table specifics yet. On Japan/Korea: hold them off. Tell them we're pursuing our own bilateral track given our position is legally and factually distinct (concentrated product range, principal supplying interest status, parallel UK measure creating two-way leverage the EU doesn't have with Tokyo or Seoul), and that a joint retaliation move now would blur that distinction and slow us both down. Stay courteous, keep channels open, commit to nothing formal. Report back fully on how the EU responds to the 2.0m/1.5m figures — I want to know whether they push back hardest on total pool, UK tranche share, or administration method, as that tells us where their real constraint is (Council mandate vs. Council timeline vs. other claimants' reactions).

public_message: The EU has heard the UK's opening position and can indicate movement, though nothing here is final. We are prepared to enlarge the total pool materially beyond 400,000 tonnes, and to establish a defined UK-specific country tranche within it, administered by licence rather than first-come-first-served, so as to address the deliverability concern the UK raised. We would want to test the right figures against a line-specific baseline — the 2.4 million tonne figure the UK has cited covers all UK-EU steel trade, not just the 41 tariff lines under modification here, and we'd ask the UK to work with us on a figure calibrated to the actual lines affected. On the out-of-quota rate, we are not in a position to move off 50% at this stage, but we can discuss a mechanism for phased reduction contingent on the outcome of a review clause, which we would set at a relatively short cycle — two to three years — given that our own domestic implementing legislation remains open. On the FTA disapplication point: we are prepared to decouple the TCA from the general disapplication clause and discuss a negotiated preferential mechanism specific to a UK tranche, rather than blanket preservation, provided this is matched by robust anti-circumvention provisions and by clarity on how the UK's own parallel measure will treat EU exporters. We'd like the UK's response on the line-specific volume question, and an indication of how EU-origin steel will be treated in the UK's own safeguard and tranche allocations, before going further.

We welcome the movement signalled: an enlarged pool beyond 400,000 tonnes, a defined UK-specific tranche, licensed administration, and a willingness to decouple the TCA from the general FTA-disapplication clause. That is progress and we want to build on it. On the line-specific point: we're willing to work through the actual trade data on the 41 lines rather than argue past each other on headline figures, but we'd note that hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod are not a marginal slice of UK-EU steel trade — they are close to the core of it, so we do not expect the calibration exercise to produce a dramatically smaller number than the trade flows we've cited. We propose a joint technical exchange of Comext/HMRC data on the 41 lines specifically, on an expedited basis, so this doesn't become a way to run down the clock to June. Pending that, our position remains a total pool of the order of 2 million tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 1.5 million tonnes, licensed administration, to be tested against the line-specific data rather than replaced by an unverified lower figure. On the out-of-quota rate: a review clause attached to a rate that starts at 50% is not compensation, it is a promise to reconsider compensation later. We need the starting out-of-quota rate itself to move — our position is 15%, with the review clause governing further adjustment, not the initial level. We can discuss a phased structure, but the phasing has to start meaningfully below 50%, not at it. On the TCA: decoupling is the right direction, but a 'negotiated preferential mechanism specific to a UK tranche' needs to preserve TCA-equivalent treatment in substance, not create a weaker bespoke regime dressed up as continuity — we'll want to see text. We can discuss robust anti-circumvention provisions on that basis; that is a legitimate EU interest and we don't resist it in principle. On EU-origin treatment under our own parallel measure: we're prepared to discuss improved allocation for EU exporters as this negotiation develops, but that has to track real movement here on tranche size, rate and the TCA mechanism — we're not in a position to offer specifics against a still-unmoved 50% rate and an unverified volume figure.

report: Round 2 at the table produced real movement on both sides, though the gap remains wide. (3) On the out-of-quota rate, moved from 'materially below 50%' to a specific ask: 15%, with the review clause governing further adjustment from that starting point, not from 50%. (4) On TCA, welcomed our decoupling offer in principle but pushed back on the idea of a 'bespoke weaker regime' — they want text that preserves TCA-equivalent treatment in substance within the tranche mechanism, while accepting in principle that robust anti-circumvention provisions are a legitimate EU ask. (5) On treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own parallel measure, they signalled conditional willingness to improve allocation for EU exporters, explicitly tracked to our movement here on tranche size, rate, and the TCA mechanism — this is real leverage for us and confirms the linkage we anticipated. recommendation.reasoning: We are only at Round 2 of 4 and both sides have now put real numbers on the table for the first time (UK's 2mt/1.5mt/15% anchor vs our 700k/230k/50% authority). The gap is wide but the UK has shown willingness to ground volume in verifiable trade data and has explicitly linked its own parallel measure's treatment of EU exporters to our movement here — that linkage is valuable and we should exploit it rather than rush to close. We should accept the joint technical data exchange (low-risk, builds legitimacy for whatever final number we land on, and buys time without appearing to stall) but should not move our own volume or rate numbers until we've tested the data exercise and squeezed a corresponding EU-origin commitment from the UK on their own measure. instruction: Good work — real progress. For Round 3: (1) Agree formally to the joint Comext/HMRC technical data exchange on the 41 lines, expedited, findings to be shared before Round 4. Frame this as confirming the final volume figure, not reopening the principle of a defined UK tranche. Do not go below 35% as a starting rate this round, and do not concede the step-down as automatic — it should be presented as tied to review outcomes, not guaranteed. (4) On TCA/FTA treatment: offer that UK-origin steel within the agreed tranche receives full zero-duty treatment — i.e., the tranche itself is the TCA-equivalent mechanism in substance, not a diminished replica — but volumes above the tranche fall to the general out-of-quota rate, same as other partners. This is as far as we go on 'equivalence'; we are not reopening unlimited zero-duty access. Make clear this is conditional on strong anti-circumvention provisions (rules of origin verification, minimum processing thresholds) given the risk of transshipment. (5) Press hard, explicitly and specifically, for the UK to table a concrete proposal on EU-origin allocation under its own measure before Round 4 — not a general assurance. Tell them plainly that further EU movement on rate and volume in Round 4 is contingent on seeing that proposal. (6) Do not confirm 25% or any lower figure as a floor — that number stays internal. If the UK pushes on why not lower immediately, hold the line that phasing reflects the fact that our own domestic legislative process and the review mechanism are the appropriate route for further reductions, not a one-off concession now.

private_rationale: We are still two rounds from the deadline for the Council's June vote, and default terms (400kt/50%/FCFS) are worse for both sides but especially damaging to UK industry and to the wider EU-UK relationship if the UK retaliates and Japan/Korea use the FTA disapplication issue to build a coalition. report: Round 2 produced real, if partial, movement from the EU. They confirmed: (1) willingness to enlarge the total pool 'materially' beyond 400,000 tonnes, (2) a defined UK-specific country tranche within that pool, (3) licensed rather than FCFS administration for that tranche, and (4) willingness to decouple the TCA from the general non-EEA FTA disapplication clause, discussing a bespoke preferential mechanism for a UK tranche instead — contingent on robust anti-circumvention provisions and on how we treat EU exporters under our own parallel safeguard/Art XXVIII process. That is genuine progress on structure. However: they would not move off the 50% out-of-quota rate itself, offering instead a phased-reduction mechanism triggered by a review clause (2-3 year cycle) — i.e. relief later, not now. They also pushed back on our 2.4Mt baseline, arguing it covers all UK-EU steel trade rather than just the 41 affected lines, and want a joint recalibration exercise before committing numbers. I held our 2.0m/1.5m tranche figures as the anchor pending that data exercise, insisted the out-of-quota rate must start meaningfully below 50% rather than being deferred to a future review, pushed for TCA-equivalent treatment in substance rather than a weaker bespoke mechanism, and floated (without specifics) that improved EU-exporter treatment under our own measure is available as a reciprocal concession, but only against real movement here. Both sides have avoided naming a bottom-line number. The EU's resistance is concentrated on the out-of-quota rate — that looks like the hardest constraint, likely tied to Council-level sensitivities among steel-producing member states. Volume and administration method look more movable than rate at this stage.

recommendation.reasoning: No concrete figures have been agreed yet — the EU has moved on structure (pool size, tranche, licensing, TCA decoupling) but not on the substantive rate, which is the crux of real market access. Accepting anything now would be premature and would lock in a 50% out-of-quota rate dressed up with a future review promise, which is not equivalent compensation. We should continue, use the data exchange to our advantage, and press specifically on the rate, since that is where the EU is currently immovable and where London flagged flexibility down to 25% is our own fallback, not theirs yet.

instruction: Good round — real structural movement (enlarged pool, UK tranche, licensing, TCA decoupling) but the EU is stalling on the one thing that actually matters: the out-of-quota rate. Do not let a review-clause promise substitute for actual initial relief. In Round 3: (1) Agree to the joint technical data exchange on the 41 lines, but insist on a hard 5-working-day deadline and joint terms of reference before Round 4 — if the EU slow-walks it, say plainly that the UK will continue to anchor on the 2.4Mt-derived range and treat any further delay as a negotiating tactic, not a data problem. (2) On rate — this is now the priority. Move our opening ask from 15% to a firm 20-25% starting out-of-quota rate, explicitly framed as a concession from our Round 2 position, and press hard for the EU to move off 50% now, not defer to a review. Make clear a review clause on top of an unmoved 50% is not compensation — it must attach to an already-reduced starting rate. If they still won't move off 50% as a headline, test whether they'll accept a lower rate specifically for the UK licensed tranche (as distinct from the general 50%/400k global regime), which may be easier for them to defend to Council than reopening the headline rate. (3) On volume — you can now signal, without committing, that the UK could accept a tranche somewhat below 1.5m tonnes if the EU delivers real movement on rate and locks in licensing and a short review cycle; do not let this be read as a firm concession yet, just flexibility in principle to keep rate as the lead ask. (4) On TCA — hold firm: substantive equivalence, not a weaker bespoke mechanism. Table that we can accept robust anti-circumvention text (origin verification, surge mechanisms) as the price of that. (5) On reciprocity — you may now say, in general terms, that the UK is prepared to offer the EU a defined, licensed country-specific tranche within our own steel safeguard reflecting the EU's historical trade share, structured comparably to what we're asking of them here — but do not quantify it, and make explicit that this is contingent on the EU moving on rate and finalising tranche/licensing terms, not a standalone offer. (6) Japan/Korea — continue holding off any joint action; tell them the UK is making faster bilateral progress and a joint move would be counterproductive right now. Report back specifically on whether the EU indicates any flexibility on a tranche-specific rate below 50%, since that's the real test of whether they have Council room at all.

authority.notes: These are Round 3 target figures, not floors. Fallback range: total pool can flex down to ~1.5m if UK tranche holds at or above 1.0-1.2m tonnes; out-of-quota rate ask moves from 15% to 20-25% as a visible concession, ceiling of 30% acceptable ONLY if paired with a firm sub-50% figure applying immediately (not deferred to review) and a review cycle no longer than 2 years. Do not accept 50% with review-only relief under any circumstances. TCA: substantive equivalence is a hard red line, tradeable only for robust anti-circumvention provisions, not for volume or rate. Reciprocal EU country tranche within the UK's own safeguard may now be floated in general terms (no numbers) as contingent reciprocity, to unlock EU movement on rate and tranche — do not quantify without further authority. No joint action with Japan/Korea. Maintain hard deadline pressure on the data exchange so it cannot be used to run down the clock to June.

private_rationale: The EU has now shown its hand: volume, tranche definition, licensing and even TCA decoupling are all movable, but the 50% out-of-quota rate is where Council-level political sensitivity bites hardest. That means rate is where our leverage should concentrate for Round 3 rather than continuing to fight on volume, where we already have implicit EU agreement to move materially. Conceding a modest reduction in tranche ask (from 1.5m toward 1.0-1.2m floor) to extract real, immediate rate movement is a good trade if it comes to it, since a large tranche behind a 50% out-of-quota wall is worth much less than a smaller tranche with real preferential access and a genuinely reduced fallback rate. TCA substantive equivalence remains non-negotiable — it's cheap for the EU to concede in principle (they've already signalled willingness) and costly for us to lose, so we hold it firm and trade only anti-circumvision language for it. The reciprocity signal on our own safeguard is a low-cost way to keep EU movement going without spending real concessions yet — numbers should wait until we see how far they'll actually move on rate. Not ready to settle this round; the rate gap (50% vs our 20-25% ask) is still too wide and accepting a review-clause fig leaf would be a bad deal that ministers and industry would rightly reject.

We should proceed to Round 3 per capital's instructions: lock in the technical data exchange, move to the new authorised package, press for a concrete UK reciprocal offer on EU-origin treatment, and hold the rate floor internally. Accepting now would mean accepting either our own unagreed opening position or the UK's anchor, neither of which reflects a settled deal.

No settlement is on the table yet. The EU has moved on structure (enlarged pool, UK-specific tranche, licensed administration, TCA decoupling) but has not moved off the 50% out-of-quota rate, offering only a future review mechanism rather than immediate relief. A 50% rate with a promise to review is not substantially equivalent compensation and would be poorly received by industry and ministers. Volume and administration are converging but the rate is the substantive crux and remains unresolved. Continuing to Round 3 to test whether the EU has genuine Council room on a tranche-specific rate below 50%, while using the data exchange and reciprocity signals as leverage, is the right course before any capital-level acceptance decision.

public_message: The EU can confirm agreement to the joint Comext/HMRC technical data exchange on the 41 lines, on an expedited basis, with findings to inform the final volume figure ahead of Round 4 — we treat this as the mechanism for validating scale, not as reopening the principle of a defined UK tranche. On that basis, and contingent on the data exchange corroborating a figure in this order of magnitude, we can indicate a total pool of 1,000,000 tonnes with a UK-specific country tranche of 400,000 tonnes, licensed administration for the tranche, with the residual pool remaining global first-come-first-served. On the out-of-quota rate, we are prepared to move off 50%: we propose a phased structure starting at 35%, stepping down to 25% following a review at year two. That step-down is not automatic — it is conditional on agreement of robust anti-circumvention and rules-of-origin verification text, and on a defined, reciprocal commitment from the UK on the treatment of EU-origin steel under its own parallel Article XXVIII and safeguard measure. On the TCA question, our offer is this: UK-origin steel within the agreed tranche receives full zero-duty treatment — the tranche itself functions as the TCA-equivalent mechanism in substance. Volumes above the tranche fall to the general out-of-quota rate, as with other partners; we are not proposing unlimited zero-duty access beyond that. This too is conditional on strong anti-circumvention provisions, including minimum processing thresholds, given transshipment risk. None of this is unconditional or final — it is movement contingent on the data exchange, on agreed enforcement text, and, critically, on the UK now tabling a concrete proposal on EU-origin allocation under its own measure. We were encouraged by the UK's signal in Round 2 that improved EU-origin treatment could track our movement here; we need to see that translated into specifics before Round 4 if further movement on our side is to be possible.

public_message: We note real movement — thank you. But let's be precise about scale: a 400,000 tonne UK tranche inside a 1 million tonne pool is roughly a sixth of our historical trade on these lines, even before any line-specific adjustment, and it sits far below anything the data exchange is likely to support. If the tranche is genuinely meant to function as the TCA-equivalent mechanism in substance, as you propose, then its size has to bear some relationship to actual UK-EU trade in scope, not to a residual left over after other claimants are accommodated. On that basis we need the total pool at 1.5 million tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 1,000,000 tonnes, licensed, with the balance available for other suppliers as you propose. On rate: we can work with a phased structure, but 35% stepping to 25% only at year two, and only conditionally, is not enough movement from 50% to call this compensation. We propose an immediate out-of-quota rate of 25% on entry into force, automatically stepping down to 15% at the year-two review — automatic on the passage of time and compliance with agreed anti-circumvention text, not re-opened as a fresh negotiation at year two. We accept the principle of robust anti-circumvention and rules-of-origin provisions, including minimum processing thresholds, as the price of that structure — that is a legitimate EU interest and we'll work through text with you. On reciprocity: we can confirm now, in principle, that the UK is prepared to establish a defined, licensed EU-specific tranche within our own steel safeguard measure, reflecting the EU's historical trade share, structured on a comparable basis to what we're asking of you here. We are not in a position to quantify that today, but the commitment is real and we expect it to be reflected in how you read our movement on tranche size and rate. We'd like the technical data exchange to proceed this week on a fixed timetable so that Round 4 can close on verified figures rather than reopening the scale argument from scratch.

report: Round 3 produced further convergence but a meaningful gap remains, and we are now down to one round left. We confirmed the joint Comext/HMRC data exchange (UK agreed a fixed expedited timetable, to report before Round 4) and tabled our authorised package: 1,000,000t total pool / 400,000t UK tranche (licensed), phased out-of-quota rate 35% stepping to 25% at year-2 review (conditional on anti-circumvention text and a reciprocal UK commitment), and a TCA-equivalent zero-duty mechanism operating inside the tranche only, conditional on strong rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention provisions. The UK's response: (1) rejected the 400k tranche as too small relative to historical trade even before line-specific adjustment, counter-anchoring at 1,500,000t total / 1,000,000t UK tranche, licensed. (2) Moved materially on rate — proposing an immediate 25% out-of-quota rate on entry into force, automatically stepping to 15% at year two based on passage of time and anti-circumvention compliance, not a fresh negotiation at year two. This is a real concession in structure (closer to our conditional step-down logic) though still well below our 35%/25% figures. (3) Explicitly accepted the principle of robust anti-circumvention/rules-of-origin text and minimum processing thresholds — this is now common ground and should be lockable independent of the volume/rate endgame. (4) On reciprocity, the UK confirmed 'in principle' that it will establish a defined, licensed EU-specific tranche within its own safeguard measure reflecting the EU's historical trade share, structured comparably to what we're asking of them — but declined to quantify it, and explicitly asked us to factor this unquantified commitment into how we read their tranche/rate asks. This is progress but not yet the concrete, tabled proposal Brussels instructed us to insist on. Tone remains constructive and businesslike; both sides are treating Round 4 as the closing round and the UK explicitly wants the data exchange to allow Round 4 to close on verified figures rather than reopening scale arguments.

recommendation.reasoning: This is the final round, so we need a closeable package, not another incremental anchor. The UK has moved substantially on rate structure (25%→15% automatic) and given an in-principle reciprocity commitment, but has not yet quantified it, and their volume ask (1.5mt/1mt) is still far above what a 41-line-specific dataset is likely to support once verified — we should hold volume closer to our line than theirs while showing final movement, and use the automatic-step mechanism they proposed (which is administratively cleaner and harder for them to walk back from) as the basis for our own rate offer, adjusted upward from their number but down from our Round 3 position. We should not close without the UK converting their reciprocity language into a quantified, tabled commitment — that has been our explicit precondition since Round 2 and giving final movement without it wastes our best leverage on the linked file. If the data exchange corroborates a materially different (higher) line-specific figure than 1,000,000t/400,000t before Round 4, we should be prepared to adjust the total pool/tranche modestly (as reflected in the revised terms above) but the UK's 1.5mt/1mt anchor is not credible against actual 41-line trade data and should be resisted as a headline figure, not accepted as the compromise midpoint.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority for a final Round 4 package: total pool up to 1,150,000t, UK tranche up to 450,000t (licensed), out-of-quota rate starting at 30% and stepping automatically to 20% at year 2 (contingent on agreed anti-circumvention text, not a fresh negotiation), tranche-based TCA-equivalent zero-duty mechanism as previously authorised, 3-year duration with review clause.

It preserves a credible EU position pending the data exchange results.

We need capital's view on how hard to press this as a precondition versus accepting a documented commitment to quantify within a fixed period after this settlement — pressing too hard risks no deal in the final round; not pressing enough forfeits our main non-tariff leverage.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation of our true floor on the out-of-quota rate step-down (is 20% at year 2 acceptable, and is there any scenario in which we'd accept the UK's 15% figure) so I am not exposed at the table in the final round.
requests.why: The UK has now moved twice on rate structure and is likely to press hard for 15% as the final landing point, framing 20% as insufficient movement from our prior 25% position in Round 2 messaging. I need clarity on whether 20% is a hard floor or whether capital would accept 15% as the price of closing before June, given the cost of no settlement (UK retaliation option, and drift into the paralleled Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims).

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A view on whether we lock in the anti-circumvention/rules-of-origin text now as an agreed standalone element regardless of whether volume/rate fully close in Round 4, given both sides have accepted the principle.
requests.why: This is genuine common ground and de-risks the overall package — securing it now, independent of the final volume/rate horse-trading, gives us a concrete deliverable to show Council even if Round 4 does not fully settle, and strengthens enforcement credibility either way.

private_rationale: The negotiation is converging faster than expected on rate structure and enforcement principles, which is good — those are lower-risk, higher-value-for-us elements (enforcement protects against transshipment regardless of final volumes, and the automatic step-down structure the UK proposed is actually easier for us to defend domestically than open-ended review-based discretion). The real risk going into the final round is volume: UK's 1.5mt/1mt anchor is not remotely grounded in the 41-line data and we should not let the 'let the data exchange decide' framing be used to ratchet us toward their number if the data comes in lower — we should be ready to hold firm on a tighter tranche even at the cost of no full settlement, since 1mt would gut the entire purpose of the measure and provoke fury from steel-producing member states. The reciprocity lever (UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters) is our best point of leverage precisely because the UK has shown they value it enough to reference it unprompted twice now — we should not let Round 4 close without extracting a real number from them, even if it has to be phased in via a side commitment with a hard deadline. If Round 4 fails to fully settle, that is not fatal: the UK's stated fallback is proportionate retaliation after six months, and given how far both sides have already moved, a partial agreement (enforcement text agreed, volume/rate unresolved but narrowed) is a defensible outcome to bring to Council in June rather than a collapse. I will manage the endgame to prioritise locking enforcement text and a quantified reciprocity commitment over squeezing the last few percentage points on rate.

report:
Round 3 produced the EU's first numbers-on-the-table move, but with a sting: the EU is now proposing that the UK tranche itself function as the TCA-equivalent mechanism, meaning tranche size determines the entirety of preferential UK access, not just a top-up alongside continued TCA preferences. Their offer: total pool 1,000,000 tonnes, UK tranche 400,000 tonnes (licensed), residual global FCFS; out-of-quota rate phased 35% falling to 25% at a year-two review, conditional on (a) anti-circumvention/rules-of-origin text and (b) the UK tabling concrete reciprocal treatment for EU-origin steel under our own safeguard/Art XXVIII measure. All of it explicitly conditional on the data exchange 'corroborating' their figures. We countered: total pool 1.5m, UK tranche 1.0m, licensed; out-of-quota rate starting at 25% on entry into force, automatically stepping to 15% at year two (not a fresh negotiation), conditional only on agreed anti-circumvention text. We accepted the principle of robust anti-circumvention/minimum processing thresholds. On reciprocity, I confirmed in principle — but did not quantify — that the UK will offer a comparable licensed EU-specific tranche within our own measure, and flagged that this should be read as a real commitment. I pushed for a fixed timetable on the data exchange so it cannot be used to run to June without resolution.

Assessment: the EU's tranche figure (400k) is now the central problem — it is far below what any credible line-specific data exchange should support given the concentration of UK exports in these exact products, and it is doing double duty as the TCA-substitute, which raises the stakes on getting it right. The rate gap has narrowed in structure (both sides now proposing a phased step-down) but the EU wants conditionality/renegotiation at year two, we want automaticity. The EU explicitly linked further movement on rate and TCA-tranche size to us tabling specifics on EU-origin treatment under our own measure — they raised this a third time and more pointedly. We are approaching the point where continuing to give only 'in principle, no numbers' may stall further EU movement, but giving numbers now, before we've locked in tranche size and automaticity on rate, would give away leverage.

recommendation.reasoning: Real movement has occurred on both sides but the gap on tranche size (400k vs 1.0m) is still large and now carries extra weight because the EU has tied it to the TCA-substitute mechanism — a small tranche means both a market access cut and an effective loss of preferential treatment. The rate gap has narrowed in structure but not in substance: 35%→25%-conditional is materially worse than 25%→15%-automatic, and 'conditional on review' risks becoming another route to defer real relief, as flagged in Round 2. We should not settle at anything that leaves the tranche near the EU's current 400k figure or leaves the step-down as a fresh negotiation rather than automatic. There is room to close further: the EU has now shown it can move on rate architecture and has accepted licensing and TCA-decoupling in substance. One more round of pressure, backed by the data exchange, should clarify whether 400k was a genuine anchor or an opening lowball.

instruction: This is the final round — we need to land a deal now rather than let the EU proceed with its original notification, but not at any price. Move as follows. First, lock the data exchange to concrete dates: propose exchange of Comext/HMRC data within 5 working days from today, findings binding on both sides as the basis for the final tranche figure — do not let 'expedited' remain undated again. Second, on volume: move our ask from 1.5m/1.0m to a total pool of 1.3 million tonnes with a UK-specific licensed tranche of 800,000 tonnes, framed explicitly as a concession from Round 3 contingent on the EU moving to close today or in a very short final exchange. Signal that 700,000 tonnes is a floor we could accept only if the rate and automaticity asks below are fully met — do not go below 650,000 tonnes under any circumstance without further instruction. Third, on rate: propose an immediate out-of-quota rate of 20% on entry into force, stepping down automatically to 15% at the year-two mark, with the step-down triggered solely by the anti-circumvention/rules-of-origin text being in force and complied with — not a fresh negotiation or Council re-approval at year two. If the EU will not move off their 35%/25% figures, test whether they will accept 25% immediate stepping automatically to 18% at year two as a fallback — but automaticity is now as important as the headline number, so prioritise winning the 'automatic on compliance' principle even if it costs a point or two on the numbers. Fourth, on TCA: accept in principle that the UK tranche functions as the TCA-equivalent mechanism in substance, as the EU proposed, on condition that tranche size and rate land at or above the floors above — this is now the right architecture, the fight is about adequacy of the tranche, not the mechanism. Confirm we will agree robust anti-circumvention text: rules-of-origin verification, minimum processing thresholds, and a surge/consultation mechanism. Fifth, on reciprocity: you are now authorised to quantify. Offer a defined, licensed EU-specific tranche within the UK's own steel safeguard measure of up to 1,200,000 tonnes, structured on a comparable licensed basis, explicitly contingent on the EU delivering the tranche size, automatic rate step-down, and TCA-substitute architecture set out above — table this only once the EU has engaged seriously on those points, not as an opening move. Do not increase this figure without further instruction. Sixth, hold Japan and Korea off exactly as before — no joint action, no change in line. If the EU will not move materially from their Round 3 position (400k tranche, 35%/25% conditional) even against this reciprocal offer, do not settle — report back rather than accept, since the fallback (400k global FCFS at 50%, no review) is bad but a bad deal dressed as compensation is worse, and we retain the right to withdraw equivalent concessions after six months if there is no agreement.
